root_theorem.statement_nl: Alice and Bob play a game with a string of $n$ digits, each of which is restricted to be $0$, $1$, or $2$. Initially all the digits are $0$. A legal move is to add or subtract $1$ from one digit to create a new string that has not appeared before. A player with no legal move loses, and the other player wins.\nAlice goes first, and the players alternate moves. For each $n \\geq 1$, determine which player has a strategy that guarantees winning.

domain_restrictions: Each coordinate/digit is an integer in the set {0,1,2}.
A legal move changes exactly one coordinate by +1 or -1, and the resulting digit must remain in {0,1,2} (no modular wrap-around).
No vertex (string) may be repeated in the play history; the initial vertex v0 is considered already visited.
Players alternate moves starting with Alice; a player with no legal move loses.
Strategies are deterministic functions of the (finite) history of the play (perfect-information, no randomness).
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n ≥ 1, the graph G_n on vertices {0,1,2}^n (edges between vertices differing by ±1 in exactly one coordinate, no wrap-around) admits a Hamiltonian path P_n starting at v0 = (0,...,0). Consequently there exists a strategy S_B for the second player (Bob), depending only on P_n, that always replies by moving to the successor along P_n of Alice's most recent vertex; this strategy is always legal and ensures Bob makes the last move. Therefore, for each n ≥ 1, Bob (the second player) has a winning strategy.
quantifier_order: for all n ∈ Z, n ≥ 1
there exists a Hamiltonian path P_n in G_n starting at v0 (i.e. ordered list visiting every vertex exactly once)
there exists a strategy S_B for Bob (which may depend on P_n and n)
for all strategies S_A for Alice (any legal play by Alice)
the play following S_A and S_B results in Bob making the last legal move (Bob wins)

witness_dependencies: The existence of Bob's winning strategy S_B for given n is witnessed by a Hamiltonian path P_n in G_n that starts at v0; P_n depends only on n, not on Alice's subsequent choices.
S_B is defined: after any Alice move to a vertex x, Bob moves to the successor of x along P_n (the vertex immediately following x in the ordering P_n).

P_n being Hamiltonian guarantees the successor exists and is unvisited at the time Bob must move, so S_B is always applicable; since |V| = 3^n is odd, the number of moves 3^n - 1 is even, so Bob (second player) makes the final move.

selected_decomposition.strategy_summary: Use the Hamiltonian-path strategy from the root sketch, but unlike the rejected attempts every lemma that mentions the graph family fully inlines the vertex set and adjacency relation, and the final game lemma states Bob's exact successor strategy with a separate first-turn and legality analysis built in.

steps.derives: For the given integer n >= 1, the graph H_n on {0,1,2}^n with unit-coordinate edges has a Hamiltonian path P_n=(v_0,v_1,...,v_{3^n-1}) starting at v_0=(0,0,...,0).
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of L4 instantiated at the chosen n.

steps.derives: For the Hamiltonian path P_n obtained in A1, every index i with 0 <= i < 3^n satisfies: the sum of the coordinates of v_i has the same parity as i.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L5 to the path P_n from A1, which starts at the all-zero vertex.

steps.derives: If Bob uses the strategy 'after Alice moves to v_i, move to v_{i+1}' along the Hamiltonian path P_n, then this strategy is always legal and guarantees that Bob makes the last move in the no-repetition game on H_n.
steps.trivial_justification: The hypotheses of L6 are exactly the facts established in A1 and A2, so L6 yields the winning property of the successor strategy.

steps.derives: For every integer n >= 1, in the game on n digits from {0,1,2} starting at (0,...,0), with legal moves changing exactly one digit by ±1 without repetition and Alice moving first, Bob has a strategy that guarantees winning.
steps.trivial_justification: From A3 we have, for an arbitrary fixed n >= 1, an explicit Bob strategy that always produces the last move. A player who makes the last legal move wins by the game rule 'a player with no legal move loses'. Since n was arbitrary, this proves the universal statement for all n >= 1, which is exactly the root theorem's conclusion.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix n >= 1 and interpret the game as play without repetition on the graph H_n whose vertices are the strings in {0,1,2}^n and whose edges are the legal one-coordinate ±1 moves. By L4, choose a Hamiltonian path P_n starting at the all-zero vertex. By L5, the i-th vertex of this path has digit-sum parity equal to i mod 2. Now define Bob's strategy exactly as in the theorem sketch: after Alice moves to some vertex of the path, Bob moves to its successor on the path. Lemma L6 applies to this path and this exact strategy, and shows both legality of every Bob reply and that Bob makes the last move. Therefore Bob has a winning strategy for every n >= 1.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let H_1 be the undirected graph with vertex set {(0),(1),(2)} and edges between two 1-tuples iff they differ by 1 in their unique coordinate. Then the ordered list ((0),(1),(2)) is a Hamiltonian path in H_1 starting at (0).

domain_restrictions: V = {(0),(1),(2)} where each element is a 1-tuple (single coordinate) taking integer values 0,1,2 respectively.
Edge relation E consists of unordered pairs {u,v} with u,v in V and |u_1 - v_1| = 1 (absolute difference of the unique coordinate is 1).
Graph is undirected, so edges are unordered pairs and adjacency is symmetric.
Hamiltonian path means an ordered sequence of vertices that (a) lists each vertex of V exactly once, and (b) consecutive entries are adjacent (their unordered pair is in E).
Adjacency only between distinct vertices (no loops).
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Define V = {(0),(1),(2)} subset of Z^1. Define E = { {u,v} : u,v in V and |u_1 - v_1| = 1 }. Let H_1 = (V,E) be the undirected graph. Let s be the sequence s_1 = (0), s_2 = (1), s_3 = (2). Then: (i) s lists each element of V exactly once (s is a permutation of V), (ii) for each i in {1,2} the unordered pair {s_i,s_{i+1}} is in E (specifically { (0),(1) } and { (1),(2) } are edges), and (iii) s_1 = (0). Therefore s is a Hamiltonian path of H_1 starting at (0).
quantifier_order: No universal/existential quantifiers over unspecified objects (declarative statement about the specific graph H_1 defined above).
Implicit: for the specific H_1 (as defined), the claim about s holds.

witness_dependencies: Existence of edge {(0),(1)}: witness is the unordered pair { (0),(1) }; it exists because |0 - 1| = 1 and both endpoints are in V. This witness depends only on the vertices (0) and (1) and the edge-definition rule.

Existence of edge {(1),(2)}: witness is the unordered pair { (1),(2) }; it exists because |1 - 2| = 1 and both endpoints are in V. This witness depends only on the vertices (1) and (2) and the edge-definition rule.
No edge {(0),(2)} is present because |0 - 2| = 2 ≠ 1; absence depends only on the same rule and the vertices (0),(2).
The claim that s is Hamiltonian depends on the two edge-witnesses above and on s enumerating all vertices of V exactly once and starting element being (0).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let the vertex set of H_1 be V = {(0),(1),(2)}. Consider the ordered list
s = ((0),(1),(2)).

To show that s is a Hamiltonian path in H_1 starting at (0), it suffices to verify three things:
1. the first vertex of s is (0);
2. s contains every vertex of H_1 exactly once;
3. consecutive vertices in s are adjacent in H_1.

First, the initial vertex of s is plainly (0), so s starts at (0).

Second, the list s contains exactly the three vertices (0), (1), and (2). These are precisely the elements of V, and they are distinct because 0, 1, and 2 are distinct integers. Hence s lists every vertex of H_1 exactly once.

Third, by the definition of the edge set of H_1, two vertices are adjacent exactly when their unique coordinates differ by 1. Now
|0-1| = 1,
so (0) and (1) are adjacent in H_1; and
|1-2| = 1,
so (1) and (2) are adjacent in H_1.
Therefore the consecutive pairs in s, namely ((0),(1)) and ((1),(2)), are edges of H_1.

Thus s is a path in H_1, it visits every vertex exactly once, and it starts at (0). Therefore s = ((0),(1),(2)) is a Hamiltonian path in H_1 starting at (0).
lemmas.role_in_parent: Base case for inductive construction of Hamiltonian paths.

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix an integer k >= 1. Let H_k be the undirected graph with vertex set {0,1,2}^k and edges between vertices that differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate, and let H_{k+1} be the analogous graph on {0,1,2}^{k+1}. Let Q=(q_0,q_1,...,q_{m-1}) be any path in H_k, meaning each q_t is a vertex of H_k and q_t is adjacent to q_{t+1} for every t<m-1. For any fixed digit a in {0,1,2}, the sequences ((a,q_0),(a,q_1),...,(a,q_{m-1})) and ((a,q_{m-1}),(a,q_{m-2}),...,(a,q_0)) are both paths in H_{k+1}. Here (a,q_t) means the (k+1)-tuple obtained by prepending a to q_t.

domain_restrictions: Vertices of H_k are k-tuples with entries in {0,1,2}; vertices of H_{k+1} are (k+1)-tuples with entries in {0,1,2}

Adjacency in H_k (and H_{k+1}) means: there exists exactly one coordinate index i such that coordinates differ and for that i the difference is ±1 (i.e. absolute difference 1), and all other coordinates are equal
The ±1 arithmetic is standard integer addition/subtraction (not modulo 3), so adjacency only occurs when the differing coordinate values remain in {0,1,2}
m is a positive integer (m ≥ 1) because indices 0..m-1 are used
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer k ≥ 1, for every path Q = (q_0,...,q_{m-1}) in H_k (m ≥ 1), and for every a ∈ {0,1,2}, the sequence P = ((a,q_0),(a,q_1),...,(a,q_{m-1})) is a path in H_{k+1}; equivalently, for each t with 0 ≤ t < m-1, the vertices (a,q_t) and (a,q_{t+1}) differ in exactly one coordinate (the same coordinate as q_t and q_{t+1}) by ±1 and hence { (a,q_t),(a,q_{t+1}) } ∈ E(H_{k+1}). Because H_{k+1} is undirected, the reversed sequence ((a,q_{m-1}),...,(a,q_0)) is also a path.
quantifier_order: For all integers k with k ≥ 1 (k fixed arbitrarily)
For all paths Q = (q_0,...,q_{m-1}) in H_k with m ≥ 1 (i.e. each q_t ∈ {0,1,2}^k and for all t with 0 ≤ t < m-1, q_t adjacent q_{t+1} in H_k)
For all digits a ∈ {0,1,2}

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix k >= 1, let Q = (q_0, q_1, ..., q_{m-1}) be a path in H_k, and fix a in {0,1,2}. We must show that both sequences
((a,q_0),(a,q_1),...,(a,q_{m-1})) and ((a,q_{m-1}),(a,q_{m-2}),...,(a,q_0))
are paths in H_{k+1}.

First consider the sequence P = ((a,q_0), (a,q_1), ..., (a,q_{m-1})).

For each t with 0 <= t <= m-1, we have q_t in {0,1,2}^k because q_t is a vertex of H_k. Since a is also in {0,1,2}, the prepended tuple (a,q_t) lies in {0,1,2}^{k+1}. Hence every term of P is a vertex of H_{k+1}.

Now fix t with 0 <= t < m-1. Because Q is a path in H_k, the vertices q_t and q_{t+1} are adjacent in H_k. Write
q_t = (x_1, ..., x_k),
q_{t+1} = (y_1, ..., y_k).
By the definition of adjacency in H_k, there exists exactly one index j in {1, ..., k} such that y_j = x_j + 1 or y_j = x_j - 1, and for every i != j we have y_i = x_i.

Then
(a,q_t) = (a, x_1, ..., x_k),
(a,q_{t+1}) = (a, y_1, ..., y_k).
These two (k+1)-tuples have the same first coordinate a. For coordinates other than j+1 they also agree, because x_i = y_i for all i != j. At coordinate j+1 they differ by exactly +1 or -1, because y_j = x_j +/- 1. Therefore (a,q_t) and (a,q_{t+1}) differ in exactly one coordinate, and in that coordinate the difference is +/- 1. By the definition of H_{k+1}, they are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

Since this holds for every t with 0 <= t < m-1, consecutive terms of P are adjacent in H_{k+1}. Thus P is a path in H_{k+1}.

Now consider the reversed sequence
P_rev = ((a,q_{m-1}), (a,q_{m-2}), ..., (a,q_0)).
Its terms are the same vertices as those of P, so each term is again a vertex of H_{k+1}. For any consecutive pair in P_rev, say
(a,q_{m-1-r}) and (a,q_{m-2-r})
with 0 <= r < m-1, the pair (a,q_{m-2-r}), (a,q_{m-1-r}) is a consecutive pair in P, hence is adjacent in H_{k+1} by the first part. Because H_{k+1} is undirected, adjacency is symmetric, so (a,q_{m-1-r}) is also adjacent to (a,q_{m-2-r}). Therefore every consecutive pair in P_rev is adjacent in H_{k+1}.

So the reversed sequence is also a path in H_{k+1}.

Hence both ((a,q_0),(a,q_1),...,(a,q_{m-1})) and ((a,q_{m-1}),(a,q_{m-2}),...,(a,q_0)) are paths in H_{k+1}, as claimed.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Justifies that each block 0·Q, 1·reverse(Q), 2·Q is internally a path in the next dimension.

lemmas.statement_nl:
Fix an integer k >= 1. Let H_k be the undirected graph with vertex set {0,1,2}^k and edges between vertices that differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate, and let H_{k+1} be the analogous graph on {0,1,2}^{k+1}. Suppose Q=(q_0,q_1,...,q_{3^k-1}) is a Hamiltonian path in H_k. Define a sequence R of vertices of H_{k+1} by concatenation:
R=((0,q_0),(0,q_1),...,(0,q_{3^k-1}),(1,q_{3^k-1}),(1,q_{3^k-2}),...,(1,q_0),(2,q_0),(2,q_1),...,(2,q_{3^k-1})).
Then R is a Hamiltonian path in H_{k+1}. Moreover, if q_0=(0,0,...,0), then the first vertex of R is (0,0,...,0) in dimension k+1.

domain_restrictions: k is an integer and k ≥ 1
Vertices of H_k are length-k tuples over {0,1,2}; vertices of H_{k+1} are length-(k+1) tuples over {0,1,2}

Adjacency in H_k and H_{k+1}: two vertices are adjacent iff they differ by exactly ±1 in exactly one coordinate (interpretation: arithmetic ±1 in Z, so allowed pairs in a coordinate are (0,1) and (1,2) and vice versa; no 0↔2 adjacency)
Q = (q_0,...,q_{3^k-1}) enumerates all vertices of H_k exactly once (q_i are pairwise distinct and |Q| = 3^k)
For 0 ≤ i < 3^k-1, q_i and q_{i+1} are adjacent in H_k
R is defined by prepending a new first coordinate (0,1,2) to entries of Q in the three blocks, with the middle block listing q_{3^k-1} down to q_0 (reverse order)
Indices run from 0 to 3^k-1 for Q and from 0 to 3^{k+1}-1 for R
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer k ≥ 1 and every Hamiltonian path Q = (q_0,...,q_{3^k-1}) in H_k (meaning the q_i are a permutation of {0,1,2}^k and q_i adjacent to q_{i+1} for 0 ≤ i < 3^k-1), define R as the concatenation R = ((0,q_0),(0,q_1),...,(0,q_{3^k-1}), (1,q_{3^k-1}),(1,q_{3^k-2}),...,(1,q_0), (2,q_0),(2,q_1),...,(2,q_{3^k-1})). Then R is a Hamiltonian path of H_{k+1}: R has length 3^{k+1}, its entries are pairwise distinct and equal exactly the set {0,1,2}^{k+1}, and for each j with 0 ≤ j < 3^{k+1}-1 the consecutive entries R_j and R_{j+1} are adjacent in H_{k+1} (i.e. differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate). Moreover, if q_0 = (0,...,0) ∈ {0,1,2}^k then the first entry of R equals (0,0,...,0) ∈ {0,1,2}^{k+1}.
quantifier_order: Fix k ∈ Z with k ≥ 1 (parameter)
Given a sequence Q = (q_0,...,q_{3^k-1}) that is a Hamiltonian path in H_k (i.e. enumerates all vertices of H_k once with successive adjacency)
Define R as the explicit concatenation depending on Q
Claim: R has the stated properties in H_{k+1}

Adjacency of consecutive vertices within each of the three blocks of R relies on adjacency of consecutive q_i in Q (within first and third blocks) or on reversed adjacency in the middle block (since middle block traverses Q in reverse)

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let m = 3^k - 1. Because Q = (q_0,q_1,...,q_m) is a Hamiltonian path in H_k, we know:
(1) q_0,q_1,...,q_m are pairwise distinct;
(2) {q_0,q_1,...,q_m} = {0,1,2}^k;
(3) for every i with 0 <= i < m, the vertices q_i and q_{i+1} differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate.

For 0 <= i <= m, define
A_i := (0,q_i), B_i := (1,q_{m-i}), C_i := (2,q_i).
Then by definition
R = (A_0,A_1,...,A_m,B_0,B_1,...,B_m,C_0,C_1,...,C_m).

We first show that R lists every vertex of H_{k+1} exactly once.
Every term of R is a (k+1)-tuple with entries in {0,1,2}, so every term is a vertex of H_{k+1}. The set of terms appearing in R is
{(0,q_i) : 0 <= i <= m} ∪ {(1,q_i) : 0 <= i <= m} ∪ {(2,q_i) : 0 <= i <= m}
= {0,1,2} × {q_0,q_1,...,q_m}
= {0,1,2} × {0,1,2}^k
= {0,1,2}^{k+1}.
Thus every vertex of H_{k+1} appears at least once in R.

To see that no vertex appears more than once, suppose (a,q_i) = (b,q_j) for some a,b in {0,1,2} and some i,j. Comparing first coordinates gives a = b. Then comparing the remaining k coordinates gives q_i = q_j. Since the q_i are pairwise distinct, i = j. Hence the terms of R are pairwise distinct. Therefore R visits every vertex of H_{k+1} exactly once. In particular, it has length 3·3^k = 3^{k+1}.

Now we show that consecutive terms of R are adjacent in H_{k+1}. There are five cases.

1. Consecutive terms inside the first block:
For 0 <= i < m, the consecutive terms are A_i = (0,q_i) and A_{i+1} = (0,q_{i+1}). Since q_i and q_{i+1} differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate of the last k positions and agree in the others, A_i and A_{i+1} differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate of a (k+1)-tuple. Hence they are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

2. Consecutive terms inside the middle block:
For 0 <= i < m, the consecutive terms are B_i = (1,q_{m-i}) and B_{i+1} = (1,q_{m-i-1}). The vertices q_{m-i-1} and q_{m-i} are consecutive in Q, so they differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate. Therefore q_{m-i} and q_{m-i-1} also differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate, and so B_i and B_{i+1} are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

3. Consecutive terms inside the third block:
For 0 <= i < m, the consecutive terms are C_i = (2,q_i) and C_{i+1} = (2,q_{i+1}). Exactly the same argument as in case 1 shows that C_i and C_{i+1} are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

4. The junction between the first and middle blocks:
The last term of the first block is A_m = (0,q_m), and the first term of the middle block is B_0 = (1,q_m). These two vertices have identical last k coordinates and differ only in the first coordinate, where 0 and 1 differ by 1. Hence they are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

5. The junction between the middle and third blocks:
The last term of the middle block is B_m = (1,q_0), and the first term of the third block is C_0 = (2,q_0). These have identical last k coordinates and differ only in the first coordinate, where 1 and 2 differ by 1. Hence they are adjacent in H_{k+1}.

So every pair of consecutive terms in R is adjacent in H_{k+1}.

We have proved that R visits every vertex of H_{k+1} exactly once and that consecutive vertices of R are adjacent. Therefore R is a Hamiltonian path in H_{k+1}.

Finally, if q_0 = (0,0,...,0) in dimension k, then the first term of R is (0,q_0) = (0,0,...,0) in dimension k+1. This proves the final assertion.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Main inductive step producing a Hamiltonian path in dimension k+1 from one in dimension k.

lemmas.statement_nl: For every integer n >= 1, if H_n denotes the undirected graph with vertex set {0,1,2}^n and edges between vertices that differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate, then H_n has a Hamiltonian path P_n=(v_0,v_1,...,v_{3^n-1}) with v_0=(0,0,...,0).

domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n >= 1 (no n = 0 case considered)
V_n = {0,1,2}^n, i.e. n-tuples with each coordinate in {0,1,2}
Edge {x,y} is in E_n iff there exists an index j in {1,...,n} with x_k = y_k for all k != j and |x_j - y_j| = 1 (integer difference, not modulo)
H_n is an undirected simple graph with vertex set V_n and edge set E_n
P_n is a sequence of length 3^n listing vertices v_0,...,v_{3^n-1} (so exactly 3^n entries)
The sequence lists each vertex exactly once (distinctness: v_i != v_j for i != j)

lemmas.proof_nl:
We prove the statement by induction on n.

Write 0^n for the all-zero n-tuple. If x=(x_1,...,x_n) is in {0,1,2}^n and a is in {0,1,2}, write (a,x) for the (n+1)-tuple (a,x_1,...,x_n).

Base case n=1:
The graph H_1 has vertex set {(0),(1),(2)} and edges {(0),(1)} and {(1),(2)}. Hence
P_1=((0),(1),(2))
is a Hamiltonian path in H_1 starting at (0)=0^1.

Induction step:
Assume for some n >= 1 that H_n has a Hamiltonian path
P_n=(u_0,u_1,...,u_{N-1}), where N=3^n,
with u_0=0^n. Because P_n is Hamiltonian, the vertices u_0,...,u_{N-1} are pairwise distinct and together equal all of {0,1,2}^n; also, for each i with 0 <= i <= N-2, the vertices u_i and u_{i+1} differ in exactly one coordinate, and in that coordinate the difference is 1 in absolute value.

Define a sequence P_{n+1} in {0,1,2}^{n+1} by
P_{n+1}=
((0,u_0),(0,u_1),...,(0,u_{N-1}),
 (1,u_{N-1}),(1,u_{N-2}),...,(1,u_0),
 (2,u_0),(2,u_1),...,(2,u_{N-1})).
We show that this is a Hamiltonian path in H_{n+1} starting at 0^{n+1}.

1. Starting vertex:
The first vertex of P_{n+1} is (0,u_0)=(0,0^n)=0^{n+1}.

2. Every vertex of H_{n+1} appears exactly once:
The vertex set of H_{n+1} is {0,1,2}^{n+1}, which is the disjoint union of the three layers
{(0,x): x in {0,1,2}^n},
{(1,x): x in {0,1,2}^n},
{(2,x): x in {0,1,2}^n}.
Since u_0,...,u_{N-1} list every element of {0,1,2}^n exactly once, the first block of P_{n+1} lists every vertex with first coordinate 0 exactly once, the second block lists every vertex with first coordinate 1 exactly once, and the third block lists every vertex with first coordinate 2 exactly once. Therefore P_{n+1} lists every vertex of H_{n+1} exactly once.

3. Consecutive vertices in P_{n+1} are adjacent in H_{n+1}:
- Inside the first block, consecutive vertices are (0,u_i) and (0,u_{i+1}) for 0 <= i <= N-2. Since u_i and u_{i+1} differ in exactly one of the last n coordinates by 1, so do (0,u_i) and (0,u_{i+1}). Hence they are adjacent in H_{n+1}.
- The last vertex of the first block is (0,u_{N-1}) and the first vertex of the second block is (1,u_{N-1}). These differ only in the first coordinate, by 1, so they are adjacent.
- Inside the second block, consecutive vertices are (1,u_i) and (1,u_{i-1}) for 1 <= i <= N-1. Since u_{i-1} and u_i are adjacent in H_n and H_n is undirected, u_i and u_{i-1} are also adjacent; therefore (1,u_i) and (1,u_{i-1}) differ in exactly one of the last n coordinates by 1, so they are adjacent in H_{n+1}.
- The last vertex of the second block is (1,u_0) and the first vertex of the third block is (2,u_0). These differ only in the first coordinate, by 1, so they are adjacent.
- Inside the third block, consecutive vertices are (2,u_i) and (2,u_{i+1}) for 0 <= i <= N-2, and the same argument as in the first block shows that they are adjacent.

Thus every consecutive pair in P_{n+1} is an edge of H_{n+1}. So P_{n+1} is a path in H_{n+1}.

By parts 2 and 3, P_{n+1} is a Hamiltonian path in H_{n+1}; by part 1, it starts at 0^{n+1}. This completes the induction step.

Therefore, for every integer n >= 1, the graph H_n has a Hamiltonian path P_n=(v_0,v_1,...,v_{3^n-1}) with v_0=(0,0,...,0).

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix an integer n >= 1. Let H_n be the undirected graph with vertex set {0,1,2}^n and edges between vertices that differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate. Let P=(v_0,v_1,...,v_{N-1}) be any path in H_n with v_0=(0,0,...,0). Then for every index i with 0 <= i < N, the sum of the coordinates of v_i has the same parity as i. In symbols, if v_i=(a_1,...,a_n), then a_1+...+a_n ≡ i (mod 2).

domain_restrictions: Vertices are length-n tuples with entries in the set {0,1,2} (integers).
Edge relation: two vertices are adjacent iff their difference vector has exactly one nonzero coordinate, and that coordinate is either +1 or -1 (so moves stay inside {0,1,2}^n).
P is a path in the graph H_n in the sense of a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent; repeats are allowed (not stated otherwise).
Index i ranges over integers 0,...,N-1. N is the number of vertices in P (≥1).
Mod 2 arithmetic is standard parity on integers.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n ≥ 1, for every path P = (v_0,...,v_{N-1}) in H_n with v_0 = (0,...,0), and for every integer i with 0 ≤ i < N, if v_i = (a_1,...,a_n) then sum_{j=1}^n a_j ≡ i (mod 2). Equivalently: the parity of the coordinate-sum of v_i equals i mod 2 for all i along any such path.

Define H_n from n (no extra quantifier; H_n is determined)
For all finite sequences P = (v_0,...,v_{N-1}) that are paths in H_n with v_0 = (0,...,0)
For all integers i with 0 ≤ i < N

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let s_i denote the sum of the coordinates of v_i. We will prove that s_i \equiv i \pmod 2 for every i with 0 \le i < N.

Write v_i=(a_1,\dots,a_n). Since v_0=(0,\dots,0), we have
s_0=0+\cdots+0=0,
so s_0 \equiv 0 \pmod 2. This proves the claim for i=0.

Now fix an index i with 0 \le i < N-1, and assume s_i \equiv i \pmod 2. We show that s_{i+1} \equiv i+1 \pmod 2.

Because P=(v_0,\dots,v_{N-1}) is a path in H_n, the consecutive vertices v_i and v_{i+1} are adjacent in H_n. By the definition of H_n, this means that there is exactly one coordinate, say coordinate t, such that the t-th coordinate changes by +1 or -1, and all other coordinates stay the same. So if
v_i=(a_1,\dots,a_n), \qquad v_{i+1}=(b_1,\dots,b_n),
then for some t we have b_t=a_t\pm 1, and for every j\ne t we have b_j=a_j.

Therefore
s_{i+1}=b_1+\cdots+b_n=(a_1+\cdots+a_n)\pm 1=s_i\pm 1.
Taking this modulo 2, and using that +1 and -1 are both congruent to 1 mod 2, we get
s_{i+1} \equiv s_i+1 \pmod 2.
By the inductive hypothesis s_i \equiv i \pmod 2, hence
s_{i+1} \equiv i+1 \pmod 2.
This completes the induction step.

By induction, s_i \equiv i \pmod 2 for all i with 0 \le i < N. Equivalently, if v_i=(a_1,\dots,a_n), then
a_1+\cdots+a_n \equiv i \pmod 2.
This is exactly the desired statement.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Gives the invariant that every Alice move lands on an odd-indexed vertex of the Hamiltonian path.

lemmas.statement_nl: Fix an integer n >= 1. Let H_n be the undirected graph with vertex set {0,1,2}^n and edges between vertices that differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate. Assume there is a Hamiltonian path P=(v_0,v_1,...,v_{3^n-1}) in H_n such that v_0=(0,0,...,0) and, for every i with 0 <= i < 3^n, the sum of the coordinates of v_i has the same parity as i. Consider the no-repetition game on H_n that starts at v_0, where Alice moves first, players alternate moving along an edge to an unvisited vertex, and a player with no legal move loses. Define Bob's strategy as follows: whenever Alice has just moved to the vertex v_i, Bob moves to v_{i+1}. Then this strategy is always legal whenever Bob is to move, and every play against any legal choices of Alice ends with Bob making the last move. Hence Bob has a winning strategy.

domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n >= 1
Vertices are n-tuples with entries in {0,1,2}; arithmetic +1/-1 changes entries within {0,1,2} (no modular wrap-around)
Edges connect two vertices exactly when they differ by ±1 in exactly one coordinate (so each edge flips parity of coordinate-sum)
P is a Hamiltonian path: P lists every vertex exactly once and consecutive terms in P are adjacent in H_n
Parity condition: for each index i, sum(v_i) ≡ i (mod 2)
Game rule: moves must follow edges and go to previously unvisited vertices; initial vertex is v_0 and Alice moves first
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any fixed integer n >= 1 and any Hamiltonian path P = (v_0,...,v_{3^n-1}) in H_n with v_0 = (0,...,0) and parity(sum of coordinates of v_i) ≡ i (mod 2) for all i, the following holds: define Bob's strategy S so that whenever Alice's last move is to the vertex v_i (i identified via P), Bob moves to v_{i+1}. Then for every legal play of the no-repetition alternating edge game starting at v_0 with Alice first, whenever Bob is to move S prescribes an adjacent vertex that has not yet been visited, and every such play ends with Bob making the final move (index 3^n-1 is even because 3^n is odd). Consequently S is a winning strategy for Bob.

Define Bob to follow strategy S: whenever Alice has just moved to some vertex v_i (i determined by P), Bob moves to v_{i+1}
Claim: For every such play against S, S prescribes a legal move whenever Bob to move, and the final move of the play is made by Bob (so S is a winning strategy for Bob).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix an arbitrary legal play of the game in which Bob follows the stated strategy. Because P=(v_0,v_1,\dots,v_{3^n-1}) is a Hamiltonian path, every vertex of H_n occurs exactly once among the v_i, so whenever Alice moves to some vertex x there is a unique index i with x=v_i. Thus Bob's rule is unambiguous whenever i+1 exists.

We first note a basic parity fact. If two vertices of H_n are adjacent, then they differ by +1 or -1 in exactly one coordinate and agree in all others. Hence the sum of the coordinates changes by \pm 1, so its parity flips on every move.

Now v_0=(0,\dots,0) has even coordinate-sum. Therefore, in any legal play starting from v_0, after each Alice move the current vertex has odd coordinate-sum, and after each Bob move the current vertex has even coordinate-sum. By the hypothesis on P, the parity of the coordinate-sum of v_i equals the parity of i. Consequently:
- every vertex Alice ever moves to is some v_i with i odd;
- every vertex Bob ever moves to is some v_j with j even.

This already shows that when Bob is to move after Alice has just moved to v_i, the index i is odd. Since 3^n is odd, the last index 3^n-1 is even. Therefore an odd index i cannot equal 3^n-1, so the successor v_{i+1} always exists.

We now prove that Bob's prescribed move is legal. Suppose Alice has just moved to v_i. As just shown, i is odd, so v_{i+1} exists. Because consecutive vertices of a Hamiltonian path are adjacent, v_i and v_{i+1} are adjacent in H_n. It remains only to show that v_{i+1} has not been visited before.

Assume for contradiction that v_{i+1} was already visited earlier in the play. Since i+1 is even, Alice could not have visited v_{i+1}, because Alice only visits odd-indexed vertices. So Bob must have visited v_{i+1} on some previous turn. But Bob's strategy sends him to v_{k+1} exactly when Alice has just moved to v_k. Therefore the only way Bob could ever move to v_{i+1} is immediately after Alice moved to v_i. So Alice would have visited v_i earlier. That contradicts the no-repetition rule, because Alice has just now moved to v_i. Hence v_{i+1} was not previously visited.

So whenever Bob is to move, his response v_{i+1} exists, is adjacent to Alice's current vertex v_i, and is unvisited. Thus the stated strategy is always legal whenever Bob is to move.

Finally, every play is finite: H_n has only 3^n vertices, and no vertex may be repeated, so there can be at most 3^n-1 moves. Since Bob always has a legal move after every Alice move, the play can never end immediately after an Alice move. Therefore, when the finite play eventually ends, it must end immediately after some Bob move. In other words, Bob makes the last move.

Hence against any legal choices of Alice, Bob's strategy is always legal and results in Bob making the last move. Therefore Bob has a winning strategy.
